lesson.title: Quick rules and their traps
lesson.subtitle: Nearest first, small swaps, and why you can’t try every plan

video.title: Quick rules and their traps
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor Eze — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Early morning: the school bus leaves the school gate; a map with nine villages around the school.
scenes.animation: The bus drives out; village dots light up one by one.
scenes.narration: Every morning our school bus picks up children in nine villages before lessons start. The driver always goes to the nearest village next. It’s quick to plan, but is it the shortest round?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: quick rules, and the traps they hide.

scenes.visual: Three rule cards, each with a small picture: a bus, a truck, a vote sheet.
scenes.animation: Cards flip over as each rule is said.
scenes.narration: A quick rule makes a plan without trying every plan. Nearest village next. Most points per kilo first. Favourite first. Quick rules are fast, easy to explain, and often good.

scenes.visual: The bus route drawn village by village; the last two legs stretch long across the map.
scenes.animation: The route grows leg by leg; the long legs flash orange.
scenes.narration: The bus rule is called nearest neighbour: from the school, drive to the closest village, then the closest one not yet visited, and so on, then back. On our map it drives thirty-four point six kilometres. But it never looks ahead, so the last legs back to school are long.

scenes.visual: Two crossing roads on the map turn dashed; the stretch between them flips and the cross disappears.
scenes.animation: Dashed roads fade; new roads draw; the total ticks down.
scenes.narration: Now improve it. Find two roads that cross, take them out, and join the stretch between them the other way round. Keep the swap if the round gets shorter. Three swaps bring it down to twenty-eight point six kilometres.

scenes.visual: A bar chart: 34.6 against 28.6; a fuel can beside the difference.
scenes.animation: Bars grow; the gap between them glows.
scenes.narration: Twenty-eight point six is the best round there is. So the quick rule drove about a fifth too far: six kilometres every morning. That’s about thirty extra kilometres of driving a week, all year.

scenes.visual: A counter of routes grows from 181,440 to a number that runs off the screen; a clock spins.
scenes.animation: Digits pile up; the clock’s hands blur.
scenes.narration: Why not just try every round? With nine villages there are one hundred and eighty-one thousand, four hundred and forty, and a computer checks those in a blink. With twenty villages there are more than a billion billion: at a billion a second, that’s about thirty-eight years. So real planners make a quick route, then improve it.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds a phone showing a finished route. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A quick rule gives me a plan in one second. What do I know about that plan?

scenes.visual: The answer card ‘Usually good, maybe not best’ gets a check; the truck lab shows 60 against 65.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; two totals slide in side by side.
scenes.narration: That it’s usually good, but maybe not the best. So check it: compare it with a better method, or try small improvements. In the truck lab, most points per kilo first gives sixty points, and the best load gives sixty-five.

scenes.visual: Inside the bus: a small child near the front, yawning, a clock above showing an hour.
scenes.animation: The clock hand sweeps a full circle.
scenes.narration: Quick rules can also be unfair. Nearest first picks up the closest children first, so they ride the bus the longest. On a long round, a small child may sit for an hour. Check who pays for a rule, not only the total.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: villages, a square for the school, the route drawing itself, a length counter.
scenes.animation: The route builds, then crossings disappear one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: The school bus route
scenes.narration: In the app, press Run and watch the bus take the nearest village each time. Then watch the swaps untangle the route. Press New map and try again: sometimes the swaps stop before the best.

scenes.visual: Amina holds up the two route drawings, tangled and untangled. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The bus round went from thirty-four point six kilometres to twenty-eight point six after three swaps. What did the swaps do?

scenes.visual: Summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: They untangled the crossing roads, and every village is still visited. Remember: quick rules are fast and often good, but not always the best. Improve a plan with small swaps. And check who a rule is hard on.

scenes.visual: A classroom: pupils standing as villages, one pupil walking with a cardboard bus sign, string on the floor showing the route.
scenes.animation: The string route straightens after a swap.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: make a human bus route. Nine pupils stand around the room as villages, and a bus pupil walks nearest first, counting steps. Then find paths that cross, swap them, and count again.

checkpoints.prompt: A quick rule gives a plan in one second. What do you know about that plan?

options.text: It is always the best plan
It is usually good, but maybe not the best

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — quick rules are usually good but make no promise. Check the plan, or improve it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a quick rule gives a plan that keeps the limits and is usually good, but there’s no promise it is the best.

checkpoints.prompt: Three swaps took the bus round from 34.6 km to 28.6 km. What did the swaps do?

options.text: They dropped a village from the round
They made the bus drive faster
They untangled crossing roads, so the round got shorter

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each swap reversed a stretch of the route to remove a crossing. Every village is still visited.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — no village was dropped and nothing got faster. Each swap reversed a stretch to remove a crossing, so the same villages are visited on a shorter round.
